title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 13
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: The Animal That Changed Distance
passages.text:
A. Of the animals humans domesticated, the horse altered human affairs most and was domesticated latest. Cattle, sheep, goats and pigs were kept for millennia before horses were, and the delay is informative: the earlier animals were taken for meat, milk and hide, and horses were initially no exception. What distinguishes the horse is a use that came later and required a different relationship — carrying a person at speed over distance.

B. Establishing when that happened is unusually difficult, because riding leaves little trace. A ridden animal is anatomically the same as an eaten one, and the equipment used need not survive. Argument has therefore relied on indirect evidence: wear on the teeth from a bit, changes in herd composition indicating breeding rather than hunting, and the geographic spread of remains beyond the animal's natural range. Each is suggestive and each has been contested, which is why proposed dates have moved by centuries as methods improved.

C. Recent evidence has come from a source that sidesteps those difficulties. Genetic material recovered from ancient remains allows populations to be compared directly, and the pattern found was not the gradual regional development that had been assumed. A single population appears to have expanded rapidly and replaced others across a vast area, carrying with it traits associated with docility and with a back structure better suited to bearing weight. The domesticated horse is, on this evidence, a recent and rapidly spread lineage rather than an accumulation of local efforts.

D. The consequences were disproportionate to the animal. Distance that had been measured in days of walking became hours of riding; a herder could manage territory that had been unmanageable; and information, disease and force all travelled faster than before. Societies with horses could act at a scale that societies without them could not match, and the resulting asymmetry shaped political geography across continents for three thousand years.

E. The relationship also imposed obligations that are easy to overlook. A horse is expensive: it competes with humans for grain, requires substantial grazing, and represents an investment that must be maintained whether or not it is currently useful. Societies that adopted horses reorganised around feeding them, and the specialised roles that grew up — breeder, farrier, groom, trainer — represent a durable diversion of labour toward maintaining a capability rather than producing food.

F. The decline of the working horse in the twentieth century was rapid and is instructive about technological replacement. Horses were not displaced by an obviously superior machine; early engines were unreliable, expensive and dependent on fuel infrastructure that did not yet exist. The transition happened as that infrastructure was built, which took decades, and during it horses and engines coexisted with each doing what it did better. Replacement was not a moment but a long overlap in which the balance of advantage shifted.

passages.title: Building for the Ear
passages.text:
The acoustic behaviour of a room was for most of architectural history a matter of accumulated craft rather than calculation. Builders knew that certain shapes and materials produced satisfactory results in halls and worship spaces, and passed the knowledge on without a theory that explained it. The transition to a predictive science happened late, and it happened because someone measured something nobody had thought to measure.

The founding quantity was reverberation time: how long a sound takes to decay to inaudibility after its source stops. Establishing it required tedious work with an organ pipe, a stopwatch and rooms full of borrowed seat cushions, and it produced a relationship simple enough to be useful — reverberation depends on the volume of the room divided by the amount of absorption within it. A hall can therefore be designed rather than attempted, and the discipline of architectural acoustics begins from that equation.

Reverberation is not a quality that should be minimised, which is the most common misunderstanding. Speech requires a short decay, because a lingering syllable overlaps the next and reduces intelligibility. Orchestral music requires a long one, because the blending of successive notes is part of what listeners understand as richness. These requirements conflict directly, which is why a hall built for one performs poorly at the other and why multi-purpose venues are usually a compromise that satisfies neither audience fully.

Absorption is only part of the problem, and the part more easily calculated. The distribution of early reflections — sound arriving within a few tens of milliseconds of the direct path — determines whether a listener perceives the source as clear and appropriately located. Reflections arriving from the sides contribute to a sense of envelopment that reflections from above do not, which is one physical reason narrow rectangular halls have a reputation that broad fan-shaped ones do not, despite the latter seating more people with better sightlines.

Certain shapes produce defects that no amount of surface treatment fully corrects. Concave curves focus sound at points, creating positions where it is unnaturally loud and others where it is dead. Parallel hard surfaces produce a rapid repeating echo audible as a buzz. Domes are acoustically difficult for the same reason as curves. These are geometric problems and require geometric solutions — diffusing surfaces, altered angles — rather than added absorption, which reduces the defect by reducing all the sound.

The modern position is that measurement and prediction are reliable and preference is not. Computer modelling predicts the physical behaviour of a proposed hall accurately, and the remaining difficulty is that the mapping from measured quantities to what listeners judge as excellent is imperfectly understood. Halls with similar measurements are ranked very differently by musicians and audiences, and the reasons include visual and cultural factors that the acoustic model does not contain.

passages.title: Why Languages Drift Apart
passages.text:
A language spoken across a large area does not stay uniform, and the reasons are structural rather than accidental. Every generation reproduces the language it hears with small deviations, and where two groups of speakers interact less with each other than with their neighbours, those deviations accumulate in different directions. Given enough time and enough separation, the accumulated differences reach the point at which mutual comprehension fails, and what were dialects are called languages.

The boundary between the two is not linguistic. Varieties that are mutually intelligible are routinely counted as separate languages where a political border runs between them, and varieties that are not mutually intelligible are counted as dialects of one language where they share a state and a writing system. Linguists describe this with the observation that a language is a dialect with an army, which is a joke about politics rather than a statement about grammar, and which describes the classification practice accurately.

Contact slows divergence and, in specific conditions, reverses it. Speakers who interact regularly converge, and the mechanism is well documented at small scale: individuals shift pronunciation toward those they are speaking with, usually without noticing, and the shift is greater toward speakers they regard positively. Where mobility increases, dialects level, and the strongest evidence for this comes from regions where transport links altered abruptly and speech patterns followed within a generation or two.

Broadcasting, which was expected to accelerate levelling, has had less effect than predicted, and the reason is instructive. Sound change appears to propagate through face-to-face interaction rather than through exposure alone, so a population hearing a prestige variety daily on screen does not adopt its vowels. What broadcast media transmit efficiently is vocabulary and idiom, which spread widely and quickly; the underlying sound system moves through networks of actual acquaintance, which is why local accents have persisted through a century of national broadcasting.

Prestige operates in two directions, and accounts that describe only the first are incomplete. Standard varieties carry overt prestige, associated with education and formal employment, and speakers shift toward them in formal settings. Local varieties carry covert prestige, associated with belonging and authenticity, and speakers shift toward them when solidarity matters more than status. The same person moves in both directions within a day, and the pattern is systematic rather than random, which is why sociolinguists can predict the direction of shift from the setting.

The persistent public assumption that language change represents decline has no support and a long history. Every documented change has been described by contemporaries as corruption, including changes now regarded as the standard from which further deviation is deplored. Change is the ordinary behaviour of a living language, and the varieties described as careless are internally regular, rule-governed and learned in exactly the way the prestige variety is learned.
